hints: Focus on what the word nucleophile actually means, a nucleus lover that seeks a positive centre.
Remember that to seek a positive centre, the particle must have electrons to offer, usually as a lone pair.
Test each option against familiar nucleophiles like $\text{OH}^-$, $\text{CN}^-$, $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to see which rule always holds.
walkthrough:
**Recall the definition**

Think of a nucleophile as an electron pair donor. It loves positive charge, so it uses its electrons to form a new bond.

General idea:
$$\text{Nu:} + \text{E}^{+} \rightarrow \text{Nu-E}$$

**Check what every nucleophile must have**

To donate electrons, every nucleophile must have a lone pair or a pi bond to give. That is the one feature they all share.

**Eliminate the not always true statements**

Many nucleophiles are neutral like $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, many are molecules not single atoms, and many attack single bonded carbons, not double bonds. Only electron pair donation is always true.

options.A: Not every nucleophile attacks a double bond. Many attack a single bonded carbon, for example $\text{OH}^-$ attacking $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$ in nucleophilic substitution. Attack on a C=C double bond is only one special case.
options.B: Correct. By definition a nucleophile donates a lone pair of electrons to an electron deficient centre (electrophile) to form a covalent bond. This is true for anions like $\text{OH}^-$ and for neutral molecules like $\text{NH}_3$.
options.C: Many nucleophiles are molecules or ions with several atoms, such as $\text{OH}^-$, $\text{CN}^-$, $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Being a single atom is not required.
options.D: Many good nucleophiles are neutral, such as $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and amines. Negative charge makes a nucleophile stronger, but it is not essential. The trap is confusing nucleophile with anion.
